newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's new government commits to tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's new government commits to tax cuts.

text.p: Ireland's newly-elected government pledged to cut taxes and spending and establish an inclusive society in which everyone can share in the fruits of economic growth, in a document outlining its Programme for Government.

The centre-right Fianna Fail/Progressive Democrat government, which officially takes office on June 26, set out its key goals for its term in office described as an 'action programme for the new millennium' late on Thursday.
It promised tax cuts by the autumn, the elimination of government borrowing and a surplus on day-to-day spending by the state.

The 27-page document, which is based on the two parties election manifestos, was ratified by Prime Minister-elect Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail party national executive and the national council of the Progressive Democrats.

The programme sets out a number key priorities to sustain economic growth, including commitments to run a current budget surplus and to eliminate exchequer borrowing over the next two to three years, if present economic conditions continue.
It said net current spending will be limited to 4.0 percent and capital spending growth to 5.0 percent on average up to 1999.
The new coalition is committing itself to cutting tax rates to 20 and 42 percent over five years, basic allowances will increase in line with inflation and the standard tax rate band will be widened.
The first instalment of tax cuts will come in the new coalition's first budget next November, it said.
The coalition included Northern Ireland, crime, drugs, education and taxation as key issues of concern to Irish people.

On Northern Ireland, the revival of the peace process and an IRA ceasefire are the key objectives and on crime there is a pledge of effective law enforcement through the controversial zero tolerance policy.
There is a strong emphasis on social issues, with the parties promising to tackle exclusion, marginalisation and poverty.

Their policy on the family, women's rights and children include the mandatory reporting of child abuse and a register of sexual offenders. There is also a strong emphasis on investment in education with primary education getting priority.
